newsitem.title: YUGOSLAVIA: Montenegro to sell off companies worth $3 bln.
newsitem.headline: Montenegro to sell off companies worth $3 bln.

text.p: Montenegro aims to offer $3 billion worth companies for sale in the next five years, but local analysts on Friday cast doubt on whether the process would develop according to plan.

The director of the State Agency for Restructuring of the Economy, Milutin Lalic, said recently that privatisation, central to Montenegro's economic strategy, was running behind target despite a favourable legal framework.
"Our set goals were quite high but the results unfortunately fall short of expectations," he told a meeting of German businessmen.
The government said an "outer wall" of sanctions barred Yugoslavia -- now comprising Serbia and Montenegro -- from access to international financial institutions.
But analysts blamed the lack of a domestic capital market for the slow pace of privatisation.
"A chronic shortage of available funds here -- almost no accumulation and lack of private capital -- has slowed privatisation," an analyst close to the government said.

"We cannot expect foreign capital to come here unless we provide the necessary prerequisites on the local market -- and that is an active financial market," he told Reuters under condition of anonymity.
He said regulated financial markets would boost local capital accumulation and savings which would be a base for future investment.

According to Lalic, the first phase of privatisation has been completed in about 350 "socially-owned" firms, those which under former Yugoslavia's unique socialist system were ostensibly owned by the workers, though in practice they were controlled by the state.
Such firms account for 80-90 percent of the republic's gross domestic product and employ 75 percent of the work force.

Under the first phase of privatisation these firms have been effectively returned to state ownership, by transferring their capital into state-controlled funds from which they must be offered for sale.
Lalic said the second phase, the search for new owners, was not proceeding as fast as the government would like.
Despite its small size, he said, Montenegro offers big opportunities for capital investment. "We expected Montenegro to become a huge building site which would lead us to dynamic development."
The government, according to Lalic, had already prepared a number of attractive investment projects in infrastructure valued at about $1.5 billion.
"Existing laws envisage all possible models of foreign capital inflow," he added.
